narrative:
The model estimated a 56.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means it judged failure slightly more likely than passing, not certain, and that estimate led to your law school application being denied.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class standing, which was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. You were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor; at 3.20 it was only slightly below the accepted-student average of 3.23, and it actually pushed toward passing, making it a relative strength. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor and also pushed toward failure: you were in the second decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile. Overall, the two low class-standing indicators outweighed the modest positive signal from your GPA.

Next, ask admissions for specific feedback, then strengthen the academic profile the model flagged. Consider additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate record showing improved performance, and seek advising on whether retaking the LSAT or applying more broadly would help. Address the third-year and first-year standing directly in any future application.
